- If sentiment is negative or near-zero in recent days, model tends to underpredict; adjust forecast upward by 1–3% to compensate for bearish sentiment bias.
- If model shows steady upward trend with no spike, but true outcome has a sharp spike later, anticipate overshoot and reduce forecast slope slightly to avoid overcorrection.
- When sentiment turns positive after a dip, model often lags; add 1–2 days of upward momentum to forecast to capture sentiment-driven rally.
- If model forecast is flat or slightly declining while sentiment is positive, increase forecast by 2–5% to reflect sentiment-driven mean reversion bias.
- For 30-day horizon, if true outcome exceeds forecast by >5% in first 5–7 days, assume momentum is strong; adjust next 5–7 days upward by 1–3% to reflect accelerating trend.
- If sentiment is positive but forecast remains flat, consider mean reversion bias — increase forecast by 1–3% to align with sentiment momentum.
- If model forecast is significantly below recent high (e.g., 78–80) and sentiment is positive, expect rebound — increase forecast by 2–5% to capture sentiment-driven reversal.
